AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
item.description:
In late October, a slew of major cybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability, which put a plethora of websites, including those of NASA, Wikipedia, the White House, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server.

As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI.

“One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche, AI security research lead at the cybersecurity startup Tolmo. “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.”

PHP Legacy Bug and Memory Errors

PHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed.

“If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana, an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University.

“It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia University

Earlier this year, the cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI. Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately.

Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.”

To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity company that confirmed and expanded the vulnerabilities) had deep knowledge of both cybersecurity and the PHP language. “I’m not claiming that AI can do it all by itself. It clearly cannot,” Jana says. “But it is improving a lot, so the top 0.1 percent [of experts] can get a lot more stuff done, and also just below the 0.1 percent now will be able to go there without understanding all the nitty-gritty details.”

AI Tools and Formal Verification in Security

After the exploits were disclosed to the PHP Foundation, a team of four engineers spent two months developing a patch to release as quickly as possible.

“There is a fundamental asymmetry in finding bugs and fixing bugs,” Jana says. “Because when you’re fixing bugs you have to make sure that you know all parts of that attack are closed, and also that you don’t break any existing functionality.”

This asymmetry puts a lot of strain on the defenders, especially for open-source software such as PHP. Maintaining open-source projects that don’t have clear revenue streams despite being widely used is a long-standing challenge that precedes AI hacking tools. But those tools make the issue more pressing than ever.

One way to stay ahead of such issues going forward is to empower the defenders with more money and access to frontier cybersecurity AI models. “These frontier labs are donating some of their token budgets to look into these bugs, which I think is great,” Jana says. “I think that should happen more, either through some concerted effort or through donations.”

Jana is also optimistic that formal verification tools to automate the patching side of the equation are also advancing quickly, including a new release from Anthropic on 22 October. “The patch is LLM-generated, and then an LLM generates the proof that the patch is correct,” says Jana. “The only thing not done by an LLM is the proof checker, because somebody has to check the proof, because LLMs hallucinate. So, you want something that is formal.”

Hopefully, the combination of specialized AI models and formal verification tools will make patching vulnerabilities nearly as automatable as finding them.

Matthew Green, an associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University Information Security Institute, is less optimistic. “Nobody’s going to fix this problem until something really bad happens,” he says. “And PHP2Shell wasn’t bad enough to be really bad. So when something really bad happens, which is going to be maybe sometime in early 2027, something bad that normal people are upset by, then suddenly people will start doing this. We’re going to fund everything.”

In the meantime, Green says, update your software. “If your phone is like, ‘Hey, there’s a security update available, do you want to install it,’ don’t wait till next week. Just do it.”

One thing’s for sure—PHP2Shell is just the beginning. “This won’t be the last one for sure,” Jana says. “It’s just who finds it. Hopefully, the white-hat hackers find it first, like this one.”

item.title: Mocktastic: A Meshtastic Node on Arduino
item.description:
Mocktastic is a small, customizable Meshtastic-compatible LoRa client for ESP32 boards using ArduinoIDE environment. It is an educational and experimental implementation, not a fork of the official Meshtastic firmware. The project demonstrates how to build and decode Meshtastic packets in C++, and includes a working environmental-sensor example.

The firmware has two compile-time modes:

DECODER provides an interactive serial shell for receiving, decoding, and sending text messages on configured Meshtastic channels and direct messages.

SENSOR turns the board into a DHT22 temperature and humidity sensor. It can send measurements and respond to /dht messages on its configured private channel.

The implementation targets the LilyGO T3 LoRa32 V1.6.1 (ESP32-PICO and SX1276) and is intended to be adapted to other compatible ESP32/LoRa hardware.

The project uses MBDTLS for the cryptographic part during the test phase and Nano-Protobuf as a lightweight protobuf encoder. The tests are written using Doctest’s lightweight C++ tests.

The repository root contains meshtastic_decoder/, which holds the firmware and host-side tests:

File or directory Purpose

meshtastic_decoder/meshtastic_decoder.ino

Arduino entry point, board integration, radio setup, and compile-time mode selection.

meshtastic_decoder/functions.h, functions.cpp

General-purpose packet, byte, and string helpers.

meshtastic_decoder/crypto.h, crypto.cpp

Cryptographic operations used by the client, including AES and X25519.

meshtastic_decoder/meshtastic.h, meshtastic.cpp

Higher-level Meshtastic packet handling, encryption, and Protobuf payloads.

meshtastic_decoder/lora_shell.h, lora_shell.cpp

Shell command parsing and high-level message operations; a good starting point when extending the client.

meshtastic_decoder/keys.h

Channel and node identity configuration.

meshtastic_decoder/nanopb_meshtastic/

Nanopb runtime and generated Meshtastic Protobuf definitions.

meshtastic_decoder/mbedtls/

The bundled mbedTLS sources used by host-side tests.

meshtastic_decoder/test/

Doctest-based unit tests for the platform-independent logic.

I used Python’s unittest approach as a model for testing individual, predictable units of logic. The project keeps protocol and utility logic separate from hardware effects so it can be exercised on a development machine. The tests themselves are written with the lightweight doctest framework and compile with bundled test dependencies.

From meshtastic_decoder, run:

cd meshtastic_decoder make test

The Makefile builds and runs the tests as one step. Tests cover the platform-independent functions, cryptography, Meshtastic packet handling, and shell parsing; changes to radio or sensor behavior should also be checked on the target hardware. To build the API documentation, install Doxygen and Graphviz, then run make doxygen from meshtastic_decoder/; the generated documentation is written to meshtastic_decoder/docs/html/.

You need an ESP32 board and a Semtech SX1276-family LoRa radio. The SENSOR variant also requires a DHT22. The tested board is the LilyGO T3 LoRa32 V1.6.1, which integrates the ESP32 and LoRa radio.

Install Arduino IDE, download or clone this repository, and open meshtastic_decoder/meshtastic_decoder.ino. Install these libraries through the Arduino Library Manager:

LoRa by Sandeep Mistry

Adafruit Unified Sensor

DHT sensor library by Adafruit

The sketch’s default is EU Medium Fast, configured as follows:

LoRa.begin(869525024); LoRa.setSpreadingFactor(9); LoRa.setSignalBandwidth(250E3); LoRa.setCodingRate4(5); LoRa.setSyncWord(0x2B); LoRa.setPreambleLength(16); LoRa.enableCrc();

Always verify local radio regulations before transmitting. In the Meshtastic documentation’s Overview page, use Radio Settings and its Frequency Slot Calculator to select a channel and slot and determine the corresponding frequency. Use that frequency in the sketch and make sure it matches the other nodes.

Before compiling, configure PublicChannel, PrivateChannel, Admn, and Device in meshtastic_decoder/keys.h:

For PublicChannel, enter the name and key of the public channel used at the selected frequency. The channel name corresponds to the radio preset (for example, MediumFast).

For PrivateChannel, enter the name and key of the private channel used for messages.

For Admn, enter the name or node ID and public key of the main node from which you will read messages. Do not put a private key in this entry.

For Device, enter this node’s name, public key, and private key.

Read the channel configuration and node details using the Meshtastic software connected to the relevant node. The Channel structure contains name and key; Friend contains name and publicKey; and User contains name, publicKey, and privateKey, in that order. Keys must be hexadecimal strings. Meshtastic may provide them in Base64; convert them to hexadecimal with b64StrToHexStr() before adding them to the configuration.

Use your own credentials and keep private keys and channel keys secret. Do not publish them in a public repository.

The sketch selects its mode at compile time. Near the top of meshtastic_decoder/meshtastic_decoder.ino, keep DECODER defined for the serial shell, or replace it with SENSOR for the DHT22 sensor variant:

#define DECODER

For the sensor build, replace that line with:

#define SENSOR

Build and upload the sketch with Arduino IDE for your selected ESP32 board.

The DECODER variant is operated over the serial connection. Open the serial monitor at 115200 baud. Its commands are:

Command Description

/echo <text>

Print text to the serial console.

/pub <text>

Send a Meshtastic packet on the public channel.

/cantine <text>

Send a Meshtastic packet on the private channel.

/admn <text>

Send a private direct message to ADMIN.

/r

Repeat the previous command.

/rssi

Show the current LoRa RSSI.

/pwr17 <value>

Set LoRa transmit power.

/gain <value>

Set LoRa gain.

/help

Show the command help.

/send_key

Start direct messaging by sending this node’s public key.

/raw <text>

Send a prepared packet for testing.

For example, send /pub 42 is the answer to write on the public channel. To send hello, world! on the private channel, use /cantine hello, world!.

To enable direct messages with Admn, first send /send_key. This sends this node’s public key so that the official Meshtastic node can establish a private conversation. Then send a direct message with /admn hello, world!.

The SENSOR variant has no interactive shell. It can only be controlled by sending a Meshtastic message on the private channel configured in keys.h. Send /dht on that channel to make the sensor measure temperature and humidity; it sends the result back as a text message on the same channel.

Connect the DHT22 data pin to GPIO 21. A battery is also required for standalone operation.

Keep protocol and parsing logic separate from hardware effects where possible. The portable logic is exercised by host-side tests, while the .ino sketch handles radio, serial, GPIO, and sensor interactions.

For a new shell command, follow the existing pattern in meshtastic_decoder/lora_shell.h and meshtastic_decoder/lora_shell.cpp: add the command to the parser and command enum, then handle it in the dispatcher in meshtastic_decoder/meshtastic_decoder.ino. For higher-level packet operations, start with the functions in lora_shell and the interfaces in meshtastic.h; use functions.h for lower-level helpers.

Run make test from meshtastic_decoder/ after changing platform-independent logic. Hardware behavior still needs to be verified on the target board and against compatible Meshtastic nodes.

This code is a learning and prototyping project. It has limited field testing, does not provide the reliability or power efficiency of the official Meshtastic firmware, and is not recommended for safety-critical or production use. Its SENSOR battery life, channel handling, and regional radio configuration may need further work for a particular application.

Guerrilla bike lanes: San Francisco makes illicit infrastructure permanent (2016)
item.description:
When two cyclists were tragically killed in hit-and-run collisions this past summer, a group of anonymous urban activists known as the San Francisco Transformation Agency erected a set of protected bike lanes using traffic cones. Usually such guerrilla interventions are temporary. They raise awareness but ultimately get taken down by municipal authorities. But when the same group recently (and illegally) installed a set of soft-hit posts alongside Golden Gate Park, the city reacted by making the change official.

The SFMTrA, a play on the city’s Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA), “is a collective organization of men and women committed to making streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians, and doing it quickly.” According to the organization, their members use tactical urbanism to accomplish a range of objectives, including:

Provide a real safety increase for cyclists and pedestrians. Draw attention to areas of the city that are unsafe for vulnerable pedestrians and cyclists. Put pressure on the SFMTA and public officials to make proactive, rapid and substantive improvements in street safety.

Many of their interventions involve orange traffic cones, which do grab visual attention but are also impermanent and easily damaged. Adding more robust traffic delineators (also known as soft or safe hit posts) may have helped persuade the city to retain this particular recent installation along John F. Kennedy Drive.

“Generally, we have no choice but to remove cones and posts that do not go through an official process,” wrote the city agency in a statement, “because it’s a code violation to place objects in the roadway, and they could create conflicts for various types of traffic.” But in this case, they plan to install official safe hit posts and leave the temporary ones in place until their review process is complete.

Guerrilla activists in other cities have tried similar things with mixed results. When the group Reasonably Polite Seattleites installed a similar set of delineators along a stretch of road in Seattle, the city initially took them down. Subsequently, though, officials wrote the activists an exceedingly nice response and eventually agreed to reinstall the posts.

City traffic engineer Dongho Chang of the Seattle Department of Transportation explained that a combination of issues (including the height of the posts and state control of the street) forced the removal at first. At the same time, he acknowledged the “time, money and risk” invested by the group and even offered to give the posts back. He later followed up with a letter indicating the city and Washington State Department of Transportation would put the delineators back in place.

In New York City, a perhaps less-polite group has been known to take things even further by building out entire bike lanes from scratch. After a local community board rejected plans to extend an extant lane, Right of Way took to the streets at night to paint their own. As a catalyst, the group cited an accident that took place after a taxi driver struck a pedestrian (after reportedly arguing with a cyclist sharing the lane).

Guerrilla interventions like these can provoke a variety of responses from critics and cities alike. In some cases, tactical urbanists are celebrated by communities but also jailed or fined by officials for their actions. In other instances, though, such installations can give a city an opportunity to publicly support a direction of change. In San Francisco, which has already built out 27 miles of protected bike lanes over recent years, the city seems to be signalling it is open to progress.

item.title: Adding Window Functions to a Spreadsheet
item.description:
Running totals, cumulative balances, and nearest matches: formulas between rows that stay correct.

Here is a formula many of us wrote early on. Put transactions in a traditional spreadsheet, like Excel or Google Sheets, one per row, and keep a running balance:

Copy the formula down, and it works. Each balance is the balance above it plus the amount on its own row.

Now you find a receipt from January 11 and insert a row for it, between rows 3 and 4. The new row has no formula, so you type one in, or copy it from above. But the balance below it now says =C3+B5. When the rows shifted, the reference was adjusted to keep pointing at the same cell, and that cell is no longer the row above. The new transaction is skipped without showing an error of any kind. The balance is just wrong from that row on.

Delete a row instead, and the formula below it becomes #REF!, and so does every balance after it.

None of this is a bug. To a traditional spreadsheet, “the previous transaction” means “the cell above”. The two agree only as long as nobody rearranges anything.

Surely there’s a better way?

There is, if you know the tricks. Vertex42 suggests OFFSET(), or a relative named range, to point at “the cell above” in a way that survives edits. Exceljet suggests a single SCAN() formula for the whole column in Excel 365.

What about the spreadsheet-like tools with database foundations? In Airtable and Baserow, a formula can only see the record it’s in, and the same goes for NocoDB and Notion databases. People asking on their forums how to do a running total in Airtable or Baserow get pointed to scripts, or to linking each record to the previous one by hand.

So these tools avoid the problem by not having a “row above” at all. But the need is there: a running balance, the days since a patient’s last visit, the stock left after each shipment.

SQL has an answer: window functions. There’s LAG and LEAD for the previous and next row, or SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY date) for a running total. They also work, but they’re an advanced tool for developers writing queries, not for people working in a table.

The actual better way: PREVIOUS()

What we really mean by “the previous row” is “the previous transaction, by date”. So let’s say exactly that. In Grist, a running balance, or any cumulative total, looks like this:

prev_balance = PREVIOUS(rec, order_by="Date").Running_Balance or 0prev_balance + $Amount

PREVIOUS(rec, order_by="Date") sorts the table by ‘Date’, finds the current record (rec), and returns the previous record. It’s a whole record (not just a cell), so .Running_Balance gets that record’s balance. The very first transaction has no previous one, so its balance comes out empty, and or 0 takes care of that.

The ordering is in the formula, not in the view. Insert a transaction anywhere, and it falls into place by its date. Delete one, and the balances close up around it. Sort the table by ‘Amount’ or filter it, and each record still holds its balance by date, because that’s what we asked for.

Now, a credit card account may have several cardholders, and each might want their own balance. You might be tempted to split the data into a table per person. Please don’t do that. Keep one table, and be specific:

prev_balance = PREVIOUS(rec, group_by="Card_Member", order_by="Date").Balance or 0prev_balance + $Amount

PREVIOUS() now finds the previous transaction by date among those of the same card member.

And since the order lives in the formula (order_by), nothing stops you from having several running totals side by side: one for the whole account, one per card member, one that starts over each month. Each column keeps its own count. Add a view linked to card members and sorted by date, and you can pick a card member and see their transactions, with their balance adding up row by row.

PREVIOUS() has two siblings. NEXT() looks the other way, and RANK() gives each record its position in the order, so RANK(rec, order_by="-Amount") <= 10 marks the ten largest transactions. The help article covers all three in more detail.

Nearest match, latest record, and effective rate

Once a lookup knows about order, “previous” is just one thing you can ask of it.

Say people’s pay rates change over time, and you keep the history: Bertha earns $110 an hour starting August 30, 2019, and $125 starting March 24, 2020. A payroll entry from February 2020 needs the rate in effect on its date, which is the latest rate that started on or before that date:

rates = Rates.lookupRecords(Person=$Person, order_by="Rate_Start")rates.find.le($Date).Hourly_Rate

lookupRecords() gets Bertha’s rates, sorted by start date. find.le() finds the last one that’s less than or equal to (that’s the le) the payroll date.

Nothing about this is specific to dates. Commission tiers work the same way: sell $5,000 and earn 7%, sell $10,000 and earn 10%, and so on.

rates = Commission_Rates.lookupRecords(order_by="Sales_Target")rates.find.le($Sales_Amount).Commission_Rate

Excel and Google Sheets users know this as an approximate match: VLOOKUP() with TRUE as the last argument. Microsoft’s own docs say the first column then needs to be sorted, and if it isn’t, “the return value might be something you don’t expect.” No error, just a different answer. In Grist, the order is part of the formula: it sorts the tiers itself, no matter how you choose to present them on the screen.

The same two lines answer a whole family of everyday nearest-match (sometimes called “approximate match”) questions:

the pay rate in effect on a given date the commission tier a sales total falls into the shipping rate for a package’s weight the tax bracket for an income the exchange rate on the day of a purchase the volume discount for an order size

And for the simplest question of all (the first or last record in a group) you don’t even need find(). Here’s a customer’s most recent order:

Orders.lookupOne(Customer=$id, order_by="-Date")

The minus sign means descending, so the first match is the latest.

The need for speed

Grist formulas are Python, so you could always write all of this by hand: get the records, loop over them, pick the right one. We should check what that costs.

A running total done by scanning, SUM(r.Amount for r in Transactions.all if r.Date <= $Date), looks at the whole table for every record. With 1,000 transactions, that’s a million steps. With 20,000, it’s 400 million.

On a test table of 20,000 transactions, PREVIOUS() computed the whole column of running balances in seconds. The scanning version was still running after five minutes.

The ordered lookups don’t scan. They keep the records sorted, and find what you ask for with a binary search, which is the fast way to do it.

All caught up

Remember when we added the receipt from January 11 and it broke the running total? In Grist, you can add it anywhere. It takes its place by date, and every balance after it recalculates. The new row’s balance is right, and so is each card member’s. Nobody has to copy a formula down, check an adjacent row, or fix an error.

That’s what you get from formulas that say what they mean: they update on their own, and they’re right every time.

For more details, see the help article Running totals, PREVIOUS, and ordered lookups. For a walkthrough of these examples, watch the webinar Advanced formulas with ordered lookups.

import openai def chat_with_preserved_thinking(client: openai.OpenAI, model_name: str): messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": "Tell me three random numbers." }, { "role": "assistant", "reasoning_content": "I'll start by listing five numbers: 473, 921, 235, 215, 222, and I'll tell you the first three.", "content": "473, 921, 235" }, { "role": "user", "content": "What are the other two numbers you have in mind?" } ] response = client.chat.completions.create( model=model_name, messages=messages, stream=False, max_tokens=4096, reasoning_effort="max", ) # the assistant should mention 215 and 222 that appear in the prior reasoning content print(f"response: {response.choices[0].message.reasoning}") return response.choices[0].message.content

item.title: Letting users trust their own MCP clients, without opening a phishing hole
item.description:
Letting users trust their own MCP clients, without opening a phishing hole The problem

You run your own agent: a Slack bot, a service on a VPS, an MCP client you wrote over a weekend. You want it on your files, which on Stream Vessel means your own S3 bucket, where an agent can read, write and delete through the MCP server. The agent speaks MCP’s standard OAuth sign-in: it registers itself, opens a browser, you click Approve, it gets a token.

It fails at step one. At registration the agent named its redirect URI, the address your browser returns to after you approve, carrying a one-time authorization code the agent swaps for a token. Yours is https://agent.yourhost.example/callback; the answer is invalid_redirect_uri. The server only accepts addresses on its operator’s allowlist: Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code and a few others. Getting yours added means asking the operator to change a config file.

The server cannot simply accept any address. That list is the addresses the post office will deliver your house keys to. Without it, a stranger registers a fake “Claude” that has the keys sent to their place, and phishes your storage with one link. So the server is either closed to you or unsafe for everyone.

Both failures are common. On the closed side, this is what people run into:

“The redirect URI is not allowed, the URL is not part of Atlassian whitelisted domains for registered MCP Clients.” — an error users, Cursor’s among them, reported in the Atlassian developer community

“…each host application must have a registered GitHub App (or OAuth App) to authenticate on behalf of the user.” — GitHub MCP server, policies and governance; otherwise you fall back to a personal access token

On the open side, a May 2026 study that tested 119 OAuth-enabled MCP servers found registration endpoints on 114 of them, 95.8%, that

“accept arbitrary redirect_uri values from anonymous requesters.”

 The attack: one link, one click, someone else’s bucket

Say your server accepts any registration and any redirect address. An attacker with no account on it can take over a user’s access in four steps:

Register a client named “Claude” whose redirect URI is https://evil.example/cb. Open registration is anonymous, by design. Send a signed-in user a normal-looking /oauth/authorize link: “Reconnect your storage to Claude”. The user sees your real consent screen, on your real domain, in their real session, and clicks Approve. The code lands at evil.example. The attacker trades it for a token and is now the user.

PKCE does not help: it lets only the client that started a flow finish it, and the attacker started this one. The client name is self-declared and proves nothing. The consent screen shows the redirect host, but claude-connect.app passes a glance. It is the same trick as the fake-app approval prompts sent to Microsoft 365 users: a real page and a real Approve; there the attacker uses an app the platform registered, here an address the server should never have accepted.

The user does approve, but on false information. A redirect allowlist is what makes an approval mean what the user thinks it means: whatever the name says, the keys can only go where the list says.

This is not hypothetical. In January 2026 Obsidian Security reported this chain against Square’s MCP server: self-registration accepted any redirect address, and one click exposed a merchant’s profile, transactions and bank details. In the researchers’ words, “any user who had previously authorized the Square MCP server was vulnerable.” Square’s fix, they note, only applied to newly registered clients.

Others found the same chain on an MCP proxy in front of a company’s single sign-on, worth a 24-hour access token and a 14-day refresh token per click, and across bug-bounty programs, where it was sometimes waved off as social engineering. SickSec’s answer: the victim never leaves the trusted domain.

A quieter problem rides along. When a request fails a check after its redirect address was accepted, the error is sent to that address. So a server that accepts any address is an open redirector on its own domain: a crafted authorize link with a bad scope bounces visitors to any site, under your hostname. RFC 9700 describes exactly this case.

What the spec says, and what servers actually do

The MCP spec names the risk and leaves the policy to each server. Its security considerations say authorization servers MUST validate exact redirect URIs, SHOULD only redirect automatically to a URI they trust, and MAY instead inform the user and let them decide. The last two are RFC 9700’s sentences, word for word. What “trust” means is left open.

Registration is shifting too. The 2026-07-28 client registration page deprecates Dynamic Client Registration (a client registering itself over an API, no human involved) for Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD), where the client id is an HTTPS URL to a document listing its redirect URIs. CIMD says who publishes a client, not whether this user meant to connect it.

The OAuth working group has been here. In a December 2025 thread on the IETF OAuth list, Warren Parad argued that unauthenticated registration turns an MCP authorization server into an open redirector. Aaron Parecki’s quoted reply points to RFC 9700 §4.11.2, which starts from exactly that setup.

In practice, servers sit at one of two poles:

Approach Example Who can connect Phishing exposure Fixed allowlist, set by the operator pgEdge Postgres MCP server: self-registration is on, but the registered URI must be on its list (Claude’s callback and two loopback URIs by default) Only listed clients; anything else needs a config change Low Whatever the client registered 114 of the 119 servers tested in the May 2026 study Any client High: the attack above

Loopback means localhost or 127.0.0.1: an app on the user’s own machine, waiting for the browser to come back.

The first pole costs real users, and clients will not fix it for you. A Claude Code issue from June 2026 reports that organizations with exact-match redirect allowlists cannot sign in from Claude Code, because its http://localhost:<port>/callback host and path are fixed. It was closed as not planned in July 2026. The server has to move.

This is not a new idea

Letting users vouch for their own app’s callback is old. GitHub has developers create an OAuth app and type in its callback URL. The MCP spec’s pre-registration option describes a server page where users register a client by hand. And an organization can add trusted redirect domains to Atlassian’s MCP server. None of these fit a client that registers itself anonymously: the first two need a client id made somewhere else, and Atlassian decides for a whole organization. So we kept self-registration and let each user decide at sign-in, for their own account, beside the server-wide list.

Our design: trust is per user, decided at sign-in

We keep the operator’s allowlist and loopback for local clients, unchanged and open to every account. On top of it, each user can trust a handful of exact https redirect addresses for their own account; ours caps at 10. On Stream Vessel that is “Trusted app addresses” on the MCP page of the web app.

The key move is when the check runs. Registration happens before anyone signs in, so it cannot know whose list to consult. So registration accepts any https URI, and the decision waits for the authorize page, where the user is known:

One rule sits under every branch: no code and no error is ever redirected to an address unless every account or this user trusts it. Before sign-in no user’s list applies, so even the OAuth library’s own validation errors (a bad PKCE challenge, an unknown scope) wait for sign-in, and a refusal is a page on our host. That closes the open-redirect hole along with the phishing one, and it covers the Deny button too: n8n’s CVE-2026-42230 (April 2026) sent users who denied consent straight to an attacker’s registered address.

Seven ways around it, each closed

Most of these rules came from trying to break the first version.

Only the user’s own browser session changes the list, never an app or API token, so a stolen token cannot widen where the user’s codes may go. Adding from the refusal page means typing the host. The page shows the host, the full address as plain text (never a link), the account it would join, and a warning: if someone sent you this link, close the page. “Trust and continue” stays disabled until the host is typed, so one click from a phishing email is not enough. The consent screen names this sign-in’s redirect, and why it is allowed. A client can register several addresses at once, so it could list claude.ai beside its own. The screen shows only the one this sign-in returns to, and its basis: on the allowlist, loopback, or “you trusted this address yourself on 3 Nov 2026”. The spec requires showing the host for metadata-document clients, though the May 2026 study found 60.5% of tested servers don’t; the basis is what makes it mean something. Every addition is emailed, and audited while the activity log is on. The email leads with the host, says when and to which account, and keeps the full address from turning into a link. It is the signal a phished user would otherwise never get. Removing an address cuts the app off, even mid-sign-in. It revokes every grant (an approval the user gave) through that address and drops codes approved but not yet exchanged. A code lives about a minute; without this, a code in flight becomes a grant after the removal. Hosts the browser and the server read differently are refused. A URI parser may keep good.example%2eevil.example as one literal host while the browser goes to good.example.evil.example. A page that names one host and sends the user to another defeats the typed-host check, so such hosts are refused at registration and on the list. Exact match only. No wildcards, no prefix match, no loopback-style port flexibility. What it does not stop, and what we turned down

It does not stop a determined social engineer: a user talked into typing an attacker’s host and approving is phished, whichever tier they pick. We bound it rather than prevent it: the typed host, the warnings, the email, instant disconnection on removal, and a consent screen that starts at read-only and says the user trusted the address.

We first capped user-trusted addresses at write access, so a phished grant could change data but not delete it. We dropped the cap: users connecting their own agents wanted full access, and the cap was a backstop, not the defense.

Beyond the two poles above, we weighed:

Option Why not on its own CIMD domain binding (redirect host must match the client id’s host) Proves who publishes the client, not that this user meant to connect it; a malicious domain can still ask “Unverified client” tier with a lower ceiling Still one click from a phishing link, at a smaller blast radius Per-user list (shipped) Needs the user’s own session to add; costs a typed host once per app
A checklist for your own MCP server Decide where codes may go at authorize, with the signed-in user known, not at registration. Check every answer, errors included, against that rule before redirecting, and refuse to a page on your own host. Do it at authorize, not only at token exchange: Cloudflare’s workers-oauth-provider shipped CVE-2025-4143 in May 2025 for checking only the latter. Show the redirect host of this request on the consent screen, and say why it is allowed. Make widening the list a deliberate act outside the sign-in flow, or behind a typed confirmation. Email the user every time an address is added. Make removal revoke grants and in-flight codes. Refuse URIs whose host the browser and your parser read differently.

Want to try it? In your own agent, add Stream Vessel’s MCP server, https://mcp.streamvessel.com, and sign in. If your agent isn’t on our list, you’ll land on the refusal page shown above, where you can trust its address and carry on.

item.title: AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history
item.description:
AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history — $17B guidance would exceed Intel's projections

AI boom drives record quarterly revenue, but client and gaming business faces double-digit declines going into 2027

AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds.

As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history.

AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year.

Data center business now accounts for 64% of AMD's revenue

AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%.

The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems.

AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025.

"We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth."

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Client revenue up, gaming revenue drops

AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter.

Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the previous quarter and up around $200 million from $2.75 billion in the same quarter a year ago.

Sales of AMD's gaming products — including discrete GPUs and system-on-chips for game consoles — dropped to $773 million from $1.298 billion in the previous year as Microsoft and Sony bought fewer console SoCs, while sales of discrete Radeon RX GPUs remained weak during the quarter. The combined segment's operating income dropped by 34% to $573 million as the unit's operating margin decreased to 15%.

"In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage," Su said. "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our rising roadmap and grow our commercial footprint."

AMD projects its Client and Gaming business to contract by more than 20% sequentially in Q4 2026 as higher memory prices weaken PC demand. The company is also preparing for a double-digit decline in PC shipments in 2027, although it expects to outperform the market by concentrating on enterprise, premium consumer, and desktop processors. Unfortunately, AMD did not provide a specific revenue forecast for its Client and Gaming segment for 2027.

Embedded business strong, set to accelerate

As for AMD's Embedded business, it also demonstrated strong growth as its revenue increased by 29% year-over-year to $1.11 billion and operating income rose by 60% to $453 million. The company attributed the improvement to stronger demand from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial customers.

AMD expects its Embedded business to grow by double digits sequentially in Q4 2026, then experience double-digit annual revenue growth over the next several years.

"Data center build-outs are also driving higher demand for our embedded CPUs and adaptive SoCs in control plane and optical networking applications," said the head of AMD. "We remain on track to close more than eighteen billion of design wins in 2026, our third consecutive record year."

Beating Intel

For those of our readers who have been following the CPU market in general as well as AMD and Intel in particular for decades, arguably the most earth-shattering part of AMD's earnings report is its outlook for the fourth quarter. The company expects revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which implies a 66% year-over-year increase and 27% sequential growth at the midpoint.

In contrast, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion amid weakening PC demand and manufacturing capacity constraints.

If AMD meets its guidance, its quarterly sales will surpass those of its considerably bigger rival Intel for the first time in history. In fact, AMD will not only leave Intel formally behond, but its projected advantage will be approximately $1.5 billion at the midpoint of both companies' forecasts, which is a tangible lead.

The development reflects the companies' increasingly different positions on the market: AMD is rapidly expanding its data center CPU and AI accelerator businesses, while Intel continues to depend heavily on PC and enterprise server processors, which sales face headwinds due to high memory prices and components shortages.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

item.title: An end to buggy web apps
item.description:
An end to buggy web apps

It is possible now to reliably and automatically detect and fix every bug which users are encountering on the web. This clearly hasn’t happened yet. Our mission at Replay is to bring it about.

A few ingredients are needed:

A modern coding agent Observability to see every bug Observability to root cause each bug A harness wiring these together

The right observability is key to this process, as it is generally to the AI powered SDLC.

Agents need context to thrive, and observability is the context layer for agents to know how the app they are building actually behaves. When they don’t actually know what is going on, they start guessing, make mistakes, and things go downhill quickly. When they do know, they can confirm theories about the app’s behavior and stay on track.

Better observability drives better results.

Perfect Observability

Replay’s core technology is a time travel debugger for Chromium and Node.js. Forked versions of these runtimes capture non-deterministic inputs to the runtimes with low overhead, allowing the runtime to be replayed deterministically. Everything it did while recording can be recovered and unpacked into what is essentially a database, allowing agents to see every statement that was executed, the state at every point, every control and data dependency, and so on, with no loss of detail.

A time travel debugger provides perfect observability: every question about how the app behaved can be answered. With one in hand, agents never need to guess. They can figure out exactly what happened, work their way back to the actual root cause of a problem, and develop the right fix.

Replay QA

We launched Replay QA a few months ago as a drop in tool for finding and explaining every bug in an app, building on our debugger. QA explores and tests apps on its own or with guidance, and with new self healing capabilities can create recordings by reproducing user sessions from partial and redacted data. It processes the recordings it creates to spot a wide variety of bugs (from broken features to glitches, performance issues, security holes and so on) and for every bug identifies the root cause and supports its analysis with evidence drawn from the recording.

QA can also fix itself. Its entire backend is recorded, and when problems are detected (failures to spot a bug or root cause it accurately) those problems are debugged, fixed, and converted to a durable test case by a software factory.

As an experiment we ran QA on 40 apps that have won contests or otherwise been promoted by major app building tools (Lovable, Replit, Base44, Bolt.new, etc). We had Astra confirm and deduplicate findings and ended up with over 900 bugs, with the distribution below.

Example: dead button

For comparison we ran other QA tools on some of these apps. Below is a bug report from QA Wolf on one of the apps, CallVance. A download button doesn’t work. QA Wolf identifies and generates STR for the bug, but does not explain at all what is causing it.

An agent addressing this bug report has to read the code and guess what the root cause is. If it guesses wrong it will have to go through several repair cycles and might end up stuck and unable to fix the problem.

These problems are not specific to CallVance or QA Wolf. The products of app building tools are loaded with bugs, and QA’ing them without using a time travel debugger can only give limited information about the causes. Surface level observations from watching screen recordings or looking at network and console logs can sometimes suggest a cause, but can’t identify it definitively, and the agent is always left guessing.

Below is a report from Replay QA for the same dead button.

Replay QA identifies the exact problem: a missing onClick handler on the React component. QA identified the rendering function associated with the button, and produced evidence showing that function and the missing handler. An agent reviewing this report can cross check the root cause against the evidence, and fix the bug itself without guessing.

Example: layout shift

The technique above applies just as well to more complex bugs, including ones that are difficult to spot without recording based analysis. Below is a layout shift in the same CallVance app. While the app loads, a skeleton changes size and other controls on the page shift around on their own, impacting usability.

Below is the root cause from the report.

This report is more extensive and describes the root cause of the layout shift in reference to all the contributing factors, including the different React commits, the network requests made in between, and variable values in the component render functions. This detailed report provides an agent exactly what it needs to fix the layout shift properly.

What’s Next

Replay QA is generally available and free to try today. It’s easy to set up integrations including self healing user session analysis, github and agent connections, and scheduled runs to keep a close watch on your app according to your needs. We are continually improving QA and are working on incorporating backend recording generation and analysis more deeply for full stack time travel debugging.

QA is also available to use via API to generate recordings and analyze them for bugs. Contact us if you’re interested in integrating its capabilities directly into a product you’re building.

item.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
item.description:
Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)

Executive summary

When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.

Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:

Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems. For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library.Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in section 6. Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system. Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees.

Today we are releasing five artifacts:

The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications; A technical report explaining the details of our system; A (Claude-written) protocol specification document; Executable code that includes: a prover and two verifiers, a fast verifier in C++, and a provably correct verifier in Lean; and Lean proofs for the top level mathematical statements, along with an interactive visualizer of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing.

We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license.1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.

Introduction

When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.

However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.

The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.

One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights.

Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference. For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).

The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.

We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development, in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees, in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators, and more.

Trust challenges in AI proliferation

The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI).

Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” (zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier, by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.

Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.

Challenge 1: pacing

Some proposals to regulate and pace AI development rely on monitoring hardware and how it is used. For example, a provider might be required to devote its hardware to inference rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference?

How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information.2 We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side.

Challenge 2: tamper detection

As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become prime targets. An attacker or rogue agent may compromise an inference server to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while hiding among genuine responses. The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers? In our Frontier Safety Roadmap, Anthropic set a public goal to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights.” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method.3

How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can require a valid zkSNARK from the server on every response. A proof is bound to a specific commitment to the weights, so it certifies not just that some model produced the response but that the committed model did. An attacker who compromises a server, or a model that substitutes itself for another, must then produce valid proofs for the expected weights to avoid detection, which they cannot do. The user may receive the proofs as well, since they leak no internal information (by zero knowledge) and are cheap to check (by succinctness); this limits what an attacker can accomplish through the inference API.

Challenge 3: text provenance

One may want to prove that considerable effort went into understanding/analyzing something. For example, a developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model. How can a user verify these claims? The user might not have the resources to run the model itself (or they might not have the clearance to do so). Even publishing the chat logs gives no absolute guarantees; a developer might in theory fake them, generating them not with a frontier model but instead with a cheaper one or a degraded version. In general, how can users verify that they are being served by their chosen model?

How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can append, along with each response, a zkSNARK proving that the output was produced by the claimed model on the given input. Succinctness lets the user check this certificate quickly, without specialized hardware, and zero-knowledge assures the provider that the user learns nothing about the proprietary weights. This complements existing mechanisms for verifying which model produced a response.

For example, in a world where exploits are being found regularly, prior to releasing new code a model provider could provide the code-developer a Proof-of-Failure that the model-provider spent at least X tokens on a specific model, and did not achieve a specific result (for example, this specific model did not find any bugs in a specific patch, after trying for at least 1M tokens).

Challenge 4: model approval

Regulation might require providers to serve only models approved as safe, rather than models deemed a cybersecurity or safety risk. A provider might have an incentive to circumvent this, since risky models might outperform competitors or be cheaper to serve. How can a regulator ensure that only approved models are served?

How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can require the provider to attach a zkSNARK to its responses, enforcing the use of approved models. The proof binds each request to the used model, so it will not verify if the provider is using an unapproved model. The regulator can check this in a lightweight way thanks to succinctness without requiring to re-execute each request.

A note on PI from trusted hardware. Prior work often focuses on trusted execution environments to achieve PI. These are hardware-based solutions that provide privacy and attestation that rely on the manufacturer producing tamper-resistant hardware. In this research, our focus is on software-only cryptographic solutions whose security and privacy relies on the hardness of computational problems. Even in the face of compromised environments (hardware, operating system and more) an adversary cannot produce a invalid proof without breaking a computationally infeasible problem. Trusted hardware and cryptography are complementary approaches with different guarantees and tradeoffs. Both will play a role in addressing the above trust challenges.

Our system: FlashProve

FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models. More details are in our technical report; here we outline the system.

FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover) and a user (the verifier). It is split into two phases:

In the offline phase, the prover publishes a commitment to the model weights, which is a short fingerprint to pin down one exact choice of weights while the weights themselves remain hidden. The later inference claims will be checked against that commitment, i.e., the weight model committed to in this phase. In the online phase, upon requests from the verifier (i.e., prompts and the corresponding output tokens), the prover produces a proof file proving the following statement:

The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated.

Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens.

Guarantees

A proof file satisfies the following “completeness” and “soundness” properties:

A proof file is accepted if it is honest (completeness). An honest prover's proof is accepted by the verifier. A proof file cannot be forged (soundness). It is effectively impossible (i.e., tantamount to breaking widely believed cryptographic assumptions) to produce a valid proof of a false statement, so the verifier does not have to trust the prover.

Completeness and soundness alone can be achieved by a computationally powerful verifier that knows the model weights (evaluate the model on the prompt and check whether the result matches the response). The next two properties are what makes the system non-trivial.

A proof file reveals nothing beyond the statement (zero-knowledge). The verifier learns nothing about the weights, the intermediate values of the computation, or which experts ran at every layer. The model architecture (excluding the weights) is not hidden. A proof file is small and cheap to check (succinctness). The attested computation is a run of a 400B-parameter (about 232 GB for a quantized version) model on an H100 GPU, while the verifier receives a proof file of about 19 MB that takes seconds to check on a 24-core CPU. An auditor, or a user with far less hardware than the provider, can check proof files without access to elaborate infrastructure. Evaluation

We measured an implementation of the protocol on Llama 4 Maverick (a 400B-parameter mixture of experts, with ~17B parameters used per token), using the publicly available 4-bit weights. Each verifier request is a window of 1,024 tokens, and each proof checks one token. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores, and the verifier on a CPU.

Prover. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores. The offline phase runs once per model and takes about 39 minutes. (For technical reasons we discuss in the technical report, the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.) The online phase, on a batch of 24 requests, takes the prover about 223 seconds, which is 110 tokens per second, and each proof is 18.78 MB. Verifier. The verifier runs on the client's CPU. It needs no GPU and only has access to a commitment to the weights. The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads (and 21 seconds on a single thread), including the offline phase's checks.

Comparison with plain inference: We ran vLLM, a widely used inference engine, with the FP8 release of the same model on eight H100s, and found that, per GPU, proving a batch of 24 requests takes about 72 times longer than vLLM takes to process the same 24 requests at once (66 to 77 across runs), and about 94 times longer when vLLM runs at the highest load we tried.

Inside the system. The underlying mechanism behind FlashProve is a zkSNARK of the kind deployed in peer-to-peer systems (e.g., L2 networks such as Starknet or Mantle for blockchains like Ethereum). Our zkSNARK is built according to a well-established recipe: an underlying information-theoretic object called an interactive oracle proof (IOP) is compiled into a cryptographic proof by relying on hash functions (and offers even post-quantum security). Our IOP is assembled from state-of-the-art building blocks using tools such as code proximity tests with linear constraints and lookup arguments, which are based on techniques from coding theory and complexity theory. Combining these pieces into a bespoke IOP for inference is a delicate task; more details about the construction can be found in the technical report.

Engineering the system

FlashProve benefits from architectural decisions that we took, and which are discussed in detail in the technical report. Here we highlight a few:

The prover's work is proportional to the experts that actually ran. In a MoE model a token uses ~17B of the 400B parameters, and the prover's work per token is proportional to those ~17B instead of all parameters (the proof still hides which experts were chosen). Requests are proved in batches, after the fact. The prover reads finished text in one parallel pass (as in prefill), and it opens the commitment to the weights once per batch instead of once per request. The system is designed to fit on a single GPU. The model weights at each layer are split to segments and are proven one segment of layers at a time. The weights are kept in ordinary memory and streamed in, so a single 80 GB GPU, with ~290 GB of host memory beside it, suffices. Post-hoc versus in-line

When integrating proving mechanisms into inference servers there is a choice: in-line proving (i.e. proving alongside the inference) versus post-hoc proving (i.e. proving after-the-fact, for a subset of tokens). Our system follows the latter. In-line solutions are expected to be ultra-fast and may sacrifice security for efficiency, whereas post-hoc solutions are allowed to be slower and may not suffer such a tradeoff. On the other hand, post-hoc proving has limitations: added complexity of recomputation, the delay in getting guarantees about your traffic, and inherent “non-determinism”. We elaborate on the motivation and implications of post-hoc proving in the technical report.

Trustworthiness from formal verification

Cryptographic code is notoriously brittle and error-prone. How can users trust the code we’re releasing today?

The answer is formal verification: we use the Lean proof assistant to specify the protocol and the desired security properties. We prove these properties in a form that is machine-checkable and guaranteed to be correct (up to compiler errors). We target three top-level properties:

Completeness: if the statement is correct, the resulting proof is accepted by the verifier. Soundness: any fake proof is rejected by the verifier (except with negligible probability). Zero knowledge: the proof reveals no information about the weights of the model, beyond what the verifier can infer from the response itself.4

These properties are stated in the so-called random oracle model, an information-theoretic way to analyze cryptographic protocols that rely on hash functions.

Formal verification leaves two important trust gaps. First, the formal statements must be audited to ensure that they match their intent. This has to be done manually (though it is dramatically less onerous than auditing proofs); we provide an interactive visualizer to assist with this.

Second, the executable code must be audited to ensure it matches the formally-defined protocol for which the security properties are proven. How to best assist with this depends on the property, because soundness depends solely on the verifier, zero-knowledge depends solely on the prover, and completeness depends on their interaction.

For soundness, we only need the verifier code to be correct (the entire value of having “proofs” is that you can fully distrust the prover if you trust the verifier). We provide an executable Lean verifier, alongside the C++ verifier. The Lean verifier runs more slowly, but Lean proves that it accepts only what the verifier in our soundness theorem accepts. Nevertheless, the C++ verifier is the one to use day to day: it carries no formal guarantee, and it agrees with the Lean verifier on every proof in our tests. For completeness, the threat model does not assume adversarial attacks (the prover and verifier are honest). Therefore, a Lean verifier lets us gain confidence through standard software testing that the honest prover produces accepting proofs: run the prover on a correct statement, and then the Lean verifier on the resulting proof. For zero knowledge, we only need the prover to be correct. However, unlike the verifier, the prover is an expensive procedure, and it would be impractical to run a Lean prover. We do not provide facilitations here: we expect that any prover that wants to hide the weights of a model they are serving has access to enough resources for careful agentic and/or human security audits to ensure equivalence to the Lean prover. Prior work

Achieving provable inference is the objective of a line of work colloquially termed “zkML”. Early works, such as SafetyNets (2017) verified a two-conv-layer MNIST CNN and a small fully connected speech model, zkCNN (2021) reached VGG-16 (15M parameters) at 88.3 s per proof, and Kang et al. (2022) proved MobileNet v2 on full-resolution ImageNet.

Transformer proofs followed: ZKML’s GPT-2 took about 159 s per token for 117M parameters (≈0.006 tok/s), and Modulus Labs’ 1.5B-parameter GPT-2 XL needed over 90 hours. EZKL (2023) proved a 1M-parameter GPT-style transformer in about 966 s per token (≈0.001 tok/s). Performance progressively improved: zkLLM (2024) proved LLaMA-2-13B on a 2,048-token input in about 15 minutes on GPU, which is ≈0.001 tok/s per new token, or ~2.5 tok/s in the batch. In 2025, zkGPT reduced GPT-2 to 21.8 s (≈0.05 tok/s), zkPyTorch proved Llama-3 8B at ~150 s per token on one CPU core (≈0.007 tok/s), and ZKTorch proved GPT-J (6B) in about 20 minutes (≈0.001 tok/s). VerInf proved Llama 4 Maverick (the same 400B-parameter MoE model we prove) at ≈0.02 tok/s. DeepProve, a current peer-reviewed state of the art, certifies an entire generated sequence with a single forward pass. It reaches about 2.9 tok/s for GPT-2 and 1.4 tok/s for Gemma 3 on one machine, and 31 tok/s distributed. SASH's prover (2026) reached ≈1.25 tok/s on Llama 3.1 8B on a single H100.

Recently commercial efforts have reached impressive numbers, with Attestable proving Gemma 4 31B at 53–77 tok/s on a single H100; at the time of writing, Attestable has not released a corresponding open source library.

The above numbers speak to the precipitous progress of provable inference in the past years. They should update our priors on what it is possible to prove in zero-knowledge.

In 2024, zkLLM proved a 13B model at about 2.5 tokens/second on one A100. The only earlier proof of Llama 4 Maverick that we know of, VerInf, reports 14.3 hours for 1,000 tokens on a DGX Spark, with a 93.6 GB proof which took almost a day to verify. FlashProve proves the same model at 110 tokens/second on a single H100, with 19 MB proofs that can be verified in seconds. Attestable independently reports 53–77 tokens/second for a dense 31B model.

We believe that the progress should transfer to more models and architectures, yielding a flexible and powerful tool with overhead over native computation of roughly 2 orders of magnitude (about 70 to 95 times in our measurements), much less than previously expected.

Limitations

This release is a research prototype, and has the following technical limitations:

No formal guarantees on fast executable code. We provide a Lean implementation of the protocol (including an executable “slow” Lean verifier), along with security properties proved in Lean. The paper and the fast executable code are derived from the Lean protocol, but we do not guarantee that all three (Lean, paper, code) match each other. The proof is about an integer model under greedy decoding. We prove an exact integer version of the published weights, and a proof asserts that each checked token is that model’s greedy choice. A reply from a floating-point implementation, or sampled decoding, could depart at some position and no longer exactly match the computation proved. The integer version is generally expected and empirically tested to be within some small error rate of true floating-point inference generically (even taking into account non-determinism of floating-point computations), though this does not cover adversarially designed prompts. Architecture hiding. Our system assumes the served model uses a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, in which each transformer layer’s feed-forward block is replaced by multiple expert sub-networks and a router that activates only a small subset of experts for each token and our system uses the MoE structure for efficiency gains. Other architectures, such as the dense models, are also widely used and its description may contain intellectual-property the model provider would like to keep secret. Indeed, one could also imagine a system that further hides the architecture of the model: the prover commits to both the weights and the architecture (i.e., the “executable code” for inference) via a hiding commitment and the verifier’s claim is about checking the execution of that committed executable on the commitment model. Side channel attacks. The current guarantee of the protocol is that the proof itself reveals nothing about the weights of the committed model. However, “side channel attacks”, such as measuring the time it takes to produce a proof, could potentially reveal information about the weights. We consider this out of scope for this release. Longer contexts. The system currently proves inference over contexts of up to 1,024 tokens. This is quite short in comparison to the contexts accumulated in chat settings. Ideally, this context length could be increased to full context windows for frontier models (which regularly have context windows of 100s of thousands to millions of tokens).
